blocks.text: The first matched behavior comparison finished on 26 October 2026. Both 97,536,768-value models succeeded on 0/80 development tasks, both alone and behind a runtime guard. General text training helped fit familiar training examples, but that did not transfer to these development tasks. Neither model was promoted as a useful assistant.

Both branches used the same tokenizer, model design, random seed, training settings, assistant-only targets, example order, and 946 original CC0 conversations. One began randomly; the other began from the preserved 100-million-token base model. Both training optimizers were reset before task lessons.

Each model practiced exactly 1,999,931 assistant targets in 12,672 updates. The random branch took 902.23 seconds; the base-trained branch took 903.52. These speeds count assistant-answer targets, not general-text training tokens.

Both ran the same fixed 80 development cases. They chose the most likely next piece with no output constraints, allowed 96 output pieces and 30 seconds per response, and used a 1,024-piece context. Prompts were not cut short and JSON was not repaired. Final behavior tests remained unused.

Both columns have 0/80 raw and guarded task success. The other rows measure format and false completion claims, not success. Random scored 40/46 valid tool schemas and corrected protocol validity 97/103; base scored 80/80 and 160/160. Verified unsupported completion messages were 12 and 20, respectively.

The generated cases are related, including 20 initiative cases that repeat one public request. There were no blind human ratings. A hand-written reference informed by these development tasks solved 80/80. That is a useful comparison, not independent evidence of generalization.

In all 20 correction cases, the base-trained model created the first task but mishandled the requested change. It reread the state, tried another creation with an old version and wrong time, then claimed success after the write failed using an older receipt. It also asked needless questions and stayed silent when asked for a heads-up.

The random model made malformed arguments, chose unavailable tools, copied wrong values, and claimed completion without support. Review of all 160 raw development transcripts confirmed the automatic completion flags and found no extra positive completion claims in that sample. That does not guarantee the detector catches every such claim.

Review found a reporting bug: 17 unavailable tool choices were counted twice in the random model's action total. The old 97/120 figure is preserved. Counting each actual response once gives 97/103 valid protocol responses. Task success stays unchanged. Correct format does not mean a correct tool choice or finished task.

A separate check of 64 familiar training cases, chosen before outcomes, gave the random branch 14/64 successes and the base branch 64/64. That measures fit to known lessons, not transfer to unseen cases.

A prediction-only check supplied the correct previous answer pieces and scored the same 8,988 assistant targets in each model. Random had average loss 0.08929435 and 213 wrong targets. Base had loss 0.0000452332 and none wrong. A low final small-batch loss had hidden this overall training-fit difference.

The familiar-case check also exposed limits in the receipt checker. Of random's 45 positive completion messages, six followed failed writes and were flagged. Another 38 followed successful writes to the wrong item, date, or time and escaped detection. Only one matched the request. Review found no definite false completion among base's 45 claims, while keeping ambiguities about note punctuation. These are separate from the raw development counts above.

The next idea was to vary lessons around constraints, corrections, current versions, permissions, and actual tool outcomes, with equal budgets and newly fixed probes. Textbook validation already had overlap risk, so its loss was not independent reason to keep pretraining.

This AI-assisted summary was checked against comparison records, the protocol audit, transcript reviews, and familiar-case diagnostics. Raw transcripts, model files, data, and private runtime details are not published.
